chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad and Ahmad ibn Muhammad, altogether from Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Ayoub, from Abu Baseer, who said:

I asked one of the two Imams (peace be upon him) about buying the (goods of) betrayal and the stolen (goods). So he (peace be upon him) said: 'No, except if there happens to have mixed up something else along with it. So as for the stolen (goods) exactly, so no, except if there happens to be goods of the Sultan (ruling authority), so there is no problem with it'.

key_terms.أَحَدَهُمَا: One of the two Imams (referring to the 5th or 6th Imam).
key_terms.السَّرِقَةِ: Theft or stealing, referring to goods taken unlawfully.
key_terms.الْخِيَانَةِ: Betrayal or treachery, often referring to goods acquired through deceit or breach of trust.
key_terms.مَتَاعِ السُّلْطَانِ: Goods of the Sultan/ruling authority, an exception to the general prohibition.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on buying stolen goods or goods of betrayal in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the fiqh of purchasing stolen goods, establishing a general prohibition unless the stolen item is mixed with legitimate property, thereby preventing total loss of ownership. It notably introduces an exception for goods belonging to the Sultan (al-Sultan), reflecting the historical Shia view of the ruler's unique authority to dispose of property or the public treasury (bayt al-mal) without the same restrictions as private individuals. This distinction highlights the interplay between private property rights and public authority in Shia jurisprudence.

en.hubeali: A number of our companions, from Sahl Bin Ziyad, and Ahmad Bin Muhammad, altogether from Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Ayoub, from Abu Baseer who said,

‘I asked one of the two (5<sup>th</sup> or 6<sup>th</sup> Imam<sup>asws</sup>) about buying the (goods of) betrayal and the stolen (goods). So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘No, except if there happens to have mixed up something else along with it. So as for the stolen (goods) exactly, so no, except if there happens to be goods of the Sultan (ruling authority), so there is no problem with it’.
en.sarwar: 1. A number of our people have narrated from Sahl ibn Ziyad and Ahmad ibn Muhammad all from ibn Mahbub from abu Ayyub from abu Basir who has said the following: “

I once asked one of the two Imam, (abu Ja’far or abu ‘Abd Allah), ‘Alayhim al-Salam, about buying goods from cheating and stealing. He (the Imam) said, ‘No, it is not lawful unless it is mixed with other goods. The very substance of stolen goods cannot be purchased unless it is of the properties of the sultan in which case it is not unlawful.’”
